bottleneck_name: Target validation / translational validity of target biology
current_state_metric: Share of all clinical failures attributed to lack of efficacy
trend_rate: Two channels moving in opposite directions. Decision-quality channel IMPROVING: human genetic support is a measured 2.6-fold relative-success multiplier and already underpins 63% of the 428 FDA approvals of 2013-2022; novel oncology target validation rose from about two per year in 2000-2004 to about ten per year in 2020-2024. Literature-reproducibility channel FLAT: no dataset shows replication rates improving. The Amgen 6-of-53 and Bayer two-thirds statistics are 2011-2012 level measurements with undisclosed selection criteria and must not be cited as trend evidence. A second active channel must also be recorded: cis-protein-quantitative-trait-locus Mendelian randomisation is a causal human instrument that does not require a trial, and its resource base has industrialised to about 2,940 plasma proteins in 34,557 UK Biobank participants [E-9549]. The countervailing empirical result travels with it: across 11,482 target-indication pairs, MR significance alone did not enrich for Phase II success while GWAS support did, so the instrument is causal in principle and not yet predictive in practice.
direct_constraint_evidence: Acts on the largest single attrition mass (40-50% of failures). Input quality is measurably poor: 6 of 53 landmark oncology papers replicated; two-thirds of Bayer validation projects inconsistent. No spare-capacity counter-evidence exists because target choice is not a capacity resource - it is a selection quality variable, so marginal return is not capped by parallelisation.
elasticity_basis: Agent D's independent flow model returns +10.19% without the budget constraint (vs my original 10.0%) and +7.05% with the industry R&D budget binding, which is D's default and the realistic case. Point set to D's budget-binding value; my unconstrained original retained as the upper bound. Derived records E-3081, E-3113.
modality_variance: Binds hardest where target biology is the whole bet: small molecule and antibody programs in CNS, immunology and metabolic disease. Binds least for vaccines (antigen validity is often known) and for cell therapy in haematology (CD19/BCMA targets already clinically validated). ADC inherits target risk from the antibody plus payload-window risk. RNA and gene therapy in monogenic disease have the lowest target risk because human genetics supplies the validation.
region_variance: Low region sensitivity; target selection is globally shared literature. China-origin programs are disproportionately fast-follower on validated targets, which lowers B1 exposure but raises commercial crowding.
notes: Rank unchanged at 1: highest elasticity and, on the evidence, still the largest attrition mass. Trend cell corrected under X-11 [E-3101] and language corrected under X-26 [E-3124]. NO LANGUAGE IN THIS ROW OR THE REPORT MAY IMPLY THAT NOTHING TECHNOLOGICAL IS BEING BROUGHT TO BEAR ON B1: the 2.6-fold genetic-support multiplier is in majority use and proteome-wide cis-pQTL Mendelian randomisation is an industrialised causal human instrument. The objection to that instrument is empirical (MR significance alone did not enrich for Phase II success), not conceptual. Both corrections change the trend and the tractability, not the rank - a factor can be improving and still be the binding constraint. Elasticity recalibrated to Agent D's budget-binding flow model [E-3113]; my original value is retained as the band's upper bound. | NON-ADDITIVE: do not sum the elasticity column; Agent D's model shows 30.5% of the naive sum of B1+B2+B8+B10 is not real [E-3115].

bottleneck_name: Preclinical-to-clinical translation (animal model predictivity, NAM validation)
current_state_metric: Fully qualified drug development tools under FDA ISTAND

trend_rate: The replacement channel moved off zero during the revision window: one tool completed FDA qualification on 8 December 2025 with the EMA opinion nine months earlier; FDA's December 2025 draft guidance removes routine six-month NHP studies for monoclonals in favour of weight of evidence, and a March 2026 draft sets four NAM validation principles
direct_constraint_evidence: Constraint is the supply of validated replacement methods, not sponsor willingness: 16 ISTAND projects have produced no qualified tool. Natural experiment available in ALS, where >100 compounds active in the mouse model showed no effect on retest and 8 had already failed in patients - relaxing reliance on that model would have prevented those trials.
elasticity_basis: Agent D returns +3.77% unconstrained (vs my original 4.0%) and +2.65% with the budget binding. Point set to D's budget-binding value. The theta lower bound is raised under red-team finding X-16 because the premise of zero qualified tools is no longer true, while remaining capped by in-silico evidence being supplemental rather than substitutive and by the EU roadmap excluding ATMPs and biologicals. Derived records E-3082, E-3113.
modality_variance: Binds hardest on small molecules and ADCs, where rodent and NHP tox studies are the gate. Binds moderately on antibodies, where species cross-reactivity often forces NHP-only tox and FDA has named mAbs as the first phase-down target. Binds least on cell and gene therapy, where animal models are already acknowledged as weakly predictive and regulators accept mechanistic and ex vivo human data. Vaccines sit in between (challenge models).
region_variance: US moving fastest on NAM acceptance (FDA roadmap, FDAMA 3.0). EU driven by REACH/3Rs but slower on drug-specific qualification. CN and JP-KR largely follow ICH; NAM-only packages face higher rejection risk outside the US, so global programs must still run the animal package.

bottleneck_name: Clinical trial patient recruitment / site capacity
current_state_metric: Activated investigative sites that under-enrol or enrol nobody
trend_rate: Enrollment interval lengthened 36.9% between 2010 and 2020; industry-to-federal oncology enrollment ratio doubled from 4.8 to 9.6 between 2008-2012 and 2018-2022
direct_constraint_evidence: REVISED - my original inference is withdrawn. I read low participation and the no-trial-locally share as evidence of usable slack; Agent F showed that reading is inverted and Agent X tested and rejected its own attack on F, so F stands. The decisive test holds screening effort constant: a deployed AI prescreening system read 98,348 charts across 29 trials, flagged 825 eligible and produced 117 enrolments - 0.12% yield after a tenfold screening-cost cut. Cheap exhaustive screening did not convert the pool because the missing resource was open matching slots. NCI-MATCH isolates the same variable inside one funded protocol: 26.4% of screened patients were matchable but 17.8% were assigned, so 8.6 percentage points of already-matched patients were lost purely to arm unavailability. The 56% no-trial-locally figure is the measurement of matched-capacity scarcity, not evidence of idleness. What survives from my original entry: the scarce resource is the matched, activated site slot rather than the patient, so remedies that add eligible patients without adding open slots do not raise output.
elasticity_basis: Cut from 2.5 on Agent D's model result: a 40% cut in enrollment duration produces exactly zero additional annual approvals (S2, S3 and S4 all return 54.45) because faster enrollment shortens the carrying period without reducing out-of-pocket spend per programme. Not cut to zero because D treats capital as exogenous with no feedback from returns onto budget. Derived records E-3083, E-3099, E-3114.
modality_variance: Binds hardest on cell and gene therapy (tiny eligible pools, few qualified treatment centres, apheresis and ICU infrastructure required) and on rare-disease RNA/gene programs. Binds moderately on oncology small molecule/ADC/antibody in biomarker-selected settings. Binds least on vaccines and on large common-disease small molecule programs, where site networks are deep and enrollment is fast.
region_variance: US site productivity is the weakest per-site and the most expensive; EU is slower to activate but more consistent per site; CN can enrol oncology trials several times faster at large centres, which is why sponsors increasingly run first-in-human in China; JP-KR sit between EU and CN with strong per-site quality but small pools.
notes: Rank falls from 7 to 10 on current-state elasticity, but this row must never be read on the current-state rank alone. Its shift rank is 1: elasticity is a function of candidate flow, and above system capacity a marginal recruitment slot buys approvals rather than time because unenrolled candidates yield exactly zero. Agent D's S7 makes Phase III patient slots the binding constraint at fivefold inflow; Agent F estimates about 60,000 additional continuously enrolling site-slots would be needed at twice current flow. Agents F and X both endorse rank ~7 at today's flow and top-three under constraint shift.

bottleneck_name: Patient-pool fragmentation from precision medicine
current_state_metric: Patients screened per enrolled participant in biomarker-selected trials
unit: ratio (2,500 HLA screens per ~38 enrollees, one cell therapy trial)
trend_rate: Subpopulation-restricted approvals have risen over the past decade to nearly match all-comer approvals, and reach market demonstrably later
direct_constraint_evidence: Screening burden is documented (NCI-MATCH screened ~6,000 patients with a 143-gene panel to fill ~40 arms). But the constraint is bidirectional: enrichment raises PoS while shrinking the pool, so 'improvement' must be defined as screening efficiency, not as less precision. No evidence found that relaxing biomarker selection raises system output; the available evidence points the other way.
elasticity_basis: Cut from 1.2 under the same D result that zeroes duration and screening-cost levers at current flow [E-3114]; the screening-efficiency definition is retained. Derived records E-3084, E-3114.
modality_variance: Binds hardest on cell therapy (HLA plus antigen plus fitness selection stacks multiplicatively) and on gene therapy for ultra-rare monogenic disease where the global pool can be under 1,000 patients. Binds strongly on ADC and targeted small molecules in oncology. Binds weakly on antibodies in broad immunology indications and negligibly on vaccines.
region_variance: CN has the largest single-country pools for common oncology biomarkers and the fastest accrual; US pools are fragmented across many competing trials; EU fragmentation is regulatory and linguistic as much as biological; JP-KR pools are small enough that ultra-rare precision trials are frequently infeasible domestically.
notes: Rank moves 10 to 11 on recalibration, not on new evidence. Agent F adds a reading my original entry missed: when the eligible population is a few thousand worldwide the Phase III is not slowed, it is replaced by a single-arm design with an external control, which transfers the binding constraint to regulatory acceptance of non-randomised evidence and books part of B4's true elasticity under B5b.

bottleneck_name: Regulatory review capacity and evidence standards (incl. AI/NAM evidence acceptance)
current_state_metric: On-time completion of FDA approval actions
trend_rate: 46 CDER novel approvals in 2025 and nearly all PDUFA commitments met despite ~3,500 staff terminated in April 2025; on-time rate slipped roughly 8-12 points in H2 2025
direct_constraint_evidence: NEGATIVE finding - the US review step has demonstrable spare capacity. Output held at 46-53 novel approvals through a 3,500-person workforce reduction, which is a natural experiment in the wrong direction: capacity was cut hard and throughput barely moved. Review also occupies roughly 10-12 months of a 9.1-year clinical span, capping any achievable gain. Where B5 does bind is evidence standards, not headcount: only 11 biomarkers and zero organ chips have completed qualification.
elasticity_basis: Parent value is the evidence-weighted blend of the two sub-rows B5a and B5b; see those rows for the separate bands. Derived records E-3085, E-3120.
modality_variance: Binds hardest on cell and gene therapy and on ADCs, where CMC review and inspection cycles dominate and where OTP/CBER capacity is thinner than CDER's. Binds least on small molecules and antibodies with conventional packages. Vaccines are region-politically sensitive rather than capacity-limited.
region_variance: US: not capacity-binding. EU: centralised procedure adds months but is predictable. CN: median ICI indication lag of 344 days behind FDA versus 118.5 days for the EU - materially binding for patient access though not for global approval count; rare-disease lag has compressed to ~1.4 years. JP-KR: PMDA and MFDS impose local-data expectations that add a development leg rather than review time.
notes: SPLIT into B5a (review capacity) and B5b (evidence standards) on Agent E's recommendation; parent row retained for continuity. Parent rank 14 to 15 on recalibration. E independently confirms the parent placement at 12th-14th and adds that the split is region-conditional: for an EU-centric portfolio B5 ranks materially higher because of the JCA gate. Japan is the cleanest counter-case in the run - the world's fastest review coexists with 86 US/EU-approved drugs nobody filed, which decouples review speed from national output.

current_state_metric: Share of clinical failures attributed to uncontrollable toxicity

Marginal-return evidence: toxicity drives roughly two-thirds of post-launch withdrawals, so each prevented late failure returns both the trial cost and the launched-asset value. Skysona's 15% malignancy rate in trial participants shows the failure mode persists in the newest modalities. Not parallelisable - a tox signal terminates the program regardless of how much capacity is available.

Binds hard on gene therapy through insertional mutagenesis and complement activation, and on cell therapy through CRS/ICANS and secondary malignancy. Binds moderately on antibodies (immunogenicity, cytokine effects) and on RNA (innate immune activation, hepatotoxicity at dose). Vaccines carry rare but reputationally decisive safety risk.
region_variance: Low region sensitivity in the biology. Regulatory tolerance differs at the margin: FDA has been more willing than EMA to accept managed risk in oncology, and CN accepts higher CAR-T toxicity thresholds in relapsed settings.

Note that dose and schedule selection, previously implicit in this row, is now carried explicitly as B17; B8 is restricted to prediction of intrinsic toxicity and immunogenicity so the two do not double-count. bottleneck_name: Wet-lab throughput (Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle)
current_state_metric: Unfilled requests for research non-human primates at US National Primate Research Centers
trend_rate: Automated platforms now report thousands of samples per day against roughly ten reactions per operator per day conventionally; but the NHP-dependent IND-enabling step remains supply-constrained, easing only in 2025-2026 as Cambodian imports resumed
direct_constraint_evidence: Split verdict. Screening and synthesis throughput show NO queueing - automation has raised capacity faster than demand, so this sub-step is fast rather than scarce and improving it further buys little. IND-enabling toxicology IS queueing: NPRCs cannot fill up to two-thirds of primate requests, most primates go to IND-enabling studies, and a single tox program is worth millions in CRO revenue, so allocation is genuinely rationed.
elasticity_basis: Parent is the blend of B9a and B9b; see those rows. Derived records E-3089, E-3118.
modality_variance: NHP dependence, and therefore the binding part of B9, is highest for antibodies and ADCs (species cross-reactivity forces NHP-only tox) and for gene therapy (NHP biodistribution).
